name: Uncal (lateral transtentorial) herniation
presentation: A patient with a growing temporal hematoma becomes drowsy, and the pupil on the side of the lesion enlarges and stops reacting to light while the eye drifts down and out. Then the opposite arm and leg weaken and the plantar becomes extensor. If nothing is done the patient becomes unresponsive, the other pupil dilates, the posture becomes extensor and breathing becomes irregular. Occasionally the weakness appears on the same side as the mass, because the opposite peduncle has been crushed against the tentorial edge.

deficits.sign: Early dilated, sluggish pupil from third nerve compression; later fixed and dilated, then bilateral
Progressive drowsiness to coma as the midbrain is displaced and compressed
Hemiparesis with extensor plantar from compression of the ipsilateral cerebral peduncle
Kernohan notch: hemiparesis on the side of the mass from compression of the contralateral peduncle against the tentorium
Occipital infarct from compression of the posterior cerebral artery against the tentorial edge

reasoning: The tentorium cerebelli separates the temporal lobes from the posterior fossa, leaving the tentorial notch through which the midbrain passes with the oculomotor nerves and the posterior cerebral arteries running beside it. An expanding lateral supratentorial mass pushes the medial temporal lobe, the uncus and parahippocampal gyrus, over the free edge of the tentorium into the notch. The first structure crushed is the oculomotor nerve, which runs forward from the midbrain beneath the uncus; its superficial pupilloconstrictor fibers fail before the motor fibers, so an enlarging, sluggish pupil on the side of the mass is the earliest sign, followed by ptosis and a down-and-out eye. The herniating uncus then presses on the cerebral peduncle, which carries the corticospinal fibers before their crossing in the medulla, so weakness appears on the opposite side; when the midbrain is instead displaced against the opposite tentorial edge, the contralateral peduncle is notched and the weakness appears on the same side as the mass, the false-localizing Kernohan sign, which is why the pupil, not the weakness, is trusted to indicate the side of the lesion. Compression and distortion of the midbrain reticular formation cause the decline in consciousness, and downward displacement stretches the paramedian perforating arteries, producing the Duret hemorrhages of the brainstem that make the late stages irreversible. The posterior cerebral artery is compressed against the tentorium, adding an occipital infarct in survivors.

imagingFindings.finding: Medial temporal lobe displaced into the suprasellar cistern, effacement of the ipsilateral ambient and suprasellar cisterns, midline shift, dilated contralateral temporal horn, midbrain rotation and widened contralateral ambient cistern.
Linear or flame-shaped hemorrhages in the midline of the midbrain and pons on SWI or CT after downward displacement.
Occipital restricted diffusion on the side of the herniation.

commonCauses: Tumor or abscess of the temporal lobe

mimics.name: Primary third nerve palsy from an aneurysm
mimics.howToDistinguish: Alert patient, no hemiparesis or altered consciousness

mimics.name: Metabolic coma
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pupils small and reactive, no lateralizing signs

mimics.name: Pontine hemorrhage
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pinpoint reactive pupils, quadriplegia, abrupt coma

management: A dilating pupil in a patient with a mass is a surgical emergency: hyperventilate briefly, give mannitol or hypertonic saline, and evacuate the mass
Head elevation, sedation, avoid hypotension and hypoxia
Intracranial pressure monitoring and decompressive craniectomy when the mass cannot be removed

imagingHint.label: uncus at the tentorial notch beside the midbrain
